entries.originalText: First keep thyself in peace, and then shalt thou be able to be a peacemaker towards others.
entries.modernizedText: First keep yourself in peace, and then you will be able to make peace with others.

entries.originalText: A peaceable man doth more good than a well-learned.
entries.modernizedText: A peaceable person does more good than a well-learned one.

entries.originalText: A passionate man turneth even good into evil and easily believeth evil; a good, peaceable man converteth all things into good.
entries.modernizedText: A passionate person turns even good into evil and easily believes evil; a good, peaceable person turns all things to good.

entries.originalText: He who dwelleth in peace is suspicious of none, but he who is discontented and restless is tossed with many suspicions, and is neither quiet himself nor suffereth others to be quiet.
entries.modernizedText: The person who dwells in peace is suspicious of no one, but the discontented and restless person is tossed about by many suspicions and is neither quiet himself nor allows others to be quiet.

entries.originalText: He often saith what he ought not to say, and omitteth what it were more expedient for him to do.
entries.modernizedText: He often says what he ought not to say and omits what it would be better for him to do.

entries.originalText: He considereth to what duties others are bound, and neglecteth those to which he is bound himself.
entries.modernizedText: He considers what duties bind others and neglects those that bind himself.

entries.originalText: Therefore be zealous first over thyself, and then mayest thou righteously be zealous concerning thy neighbour.
entries.modernizedText: Therefore, be zealous first over yourself, and then you may rightly be zealous concerning your neighbor.

entries.originalText: Thou knowest well how to excuse and to colour thine own deeds, but thou wilt not accept the excuses of others.
entries.modernizedText: You know well how to excuse and make your own deeds look better, but you will not accept the excuses of others.

entries.originalText: It would be more just to accuse thyself and excuse thy brother.
entries.modernizedText: It would be more just to accuse yourself and excuse your brother.

entries.originalText: If thou wilt that others bear with thee, bear thou with others.
entries.modernizedText: If you want others to bear with you, bear with others.

entries.originalText: Behold how far thou art as yet from the true charity and humility which knows not how to be angry or indignant against any save self alone.
entries.modernizedText: See how far you still are from the true charity and humility that cannot be angry or indignant with anyone except self alone.

entries.originalText: It is no great thing to mingle with the good and the meek, for this is naturally pleasing to all, and every one of us willingly enjoyeth peace and liketh best those who think with us: but to be able to live peaceably with the hard and perverse, or with the disorderly, or those who oppose us, this is a great grace and a thing much to be commended and most worthy of a man.
entries.modernizedText: It is no great thing to associate with the good and the meek, for this is naturally pleasing to all, and each of us willingly enjoys peace and likes best those who think as we do. But to be able to live peaceably with the hard and perverse, or with the disorderly, or those who oppose us, is a great grace, much to be commended and most worthy of a person.

entries.originalText: There are who keep themselves in peace and keep peace also with others, and there are who neither have peace nor suffer others to have peace; they are troublesome to others, but always more troublesome to themselves.
entries.modernizedText: Some keep themselves in peace and keep peace with others also, and some neither have peace nor allow others to have peace; they are troublesome to others, but always more troublesome to themselves.

entries.originalText: And there are who hold themselves in peace, and study to bring others unto peace; nevertheless, all our peace in this sad life lieth in humble suffering rather than in not feeling adversities.
entries.modernizedText: And some keep themselves in peace and strive to bring others to peace; nevertheless, all our peace in this sad life lies in humble suffering rather than in not feeling adversities.

entries.originalText: He who best knoweth how to suffer shall possess the most peace; that man is conqueror of himself and lord of the world, the friend of Christ, and the inheritor of heaven.
entries.modernizedText: The person who best knows how to suffer will possess the most peace; that person is conqueror of himself and lord of the world, the friend of Christ, and the inheritor of heaven.
